title: Sliding Window Median
prompt:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. There is a sliding window of size `k` which moves from the very left of the array to the very right, one position at a time. For each window position, compute the median of the `k` elements currently inside it.

The median of an array of size `k` is the middle element if `k` is odd, or the average of the two middle elements if `k` is even. Return an array of the medians for every window position, in order.

examples.explanation: Window [1,3,-1] -> median 1. Window [3,-1,-3] -> median -1. Window [-1,-3,5] -> median -1. And so on as the window slides.

hints: Recomputing the median by sorting each window from scratch costs O(k log k) per window, or O(n*k log k) overall — far too slow for large inputs.
Maintain two balanced heaps, like in the median-of-a-data-stream problem: a max-heap for the smaller half of the current window and a min-heap for the larger half, kept equal size (or off by one).

The tricky new part is removal: when the window slides, an old element must leave. Use 'lazy deletion' — mark elements as removed in a hash map and only actually pop them from a heap when they surface at the top, rebalancing heap sizes to account for pending removals.

solution.approach: Extend the two-heap median technique with lazy deletion to support removing elements as the window slides. Maintain a max-heap `small` (smaller half, negated) and a min-heap `large` (larger half), plus a hash map counting elements pending removal. When adding a new element, insert it into the correct heap and rebalance sizes. When removing the outgoing element, decrement its pending-removal count and, if it happens to sit at the top of either heap, pop it immediately along with any other stale top elements; otherwise just adjust a size-tracking balance so future rebalancing accounts for the fact that heap holds a 'ghost' entry. After each insert/remove pair, the median is read the same way as in the streaming median problem: the top of `small` if it has more real elements, or the average of both tops if balanced.
